title: Andy Taylor, original guitarist for Duran Duran, dies at 65 | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Andy Taylor, an original member of Duran Duran whose distinctive guitar riffs shaped many of the iconic ‘80s new wave band’s biggest hits — including “Rio” and “The Reflex” — has died. He was65.

The news was confirmed on theofficial Instagram accountfor Duran Duran, where a statement said that Taylor died peacefully at home surrounded by his family on Monday. The band’s lead singer Simon Le Bon added on theband’s official site, “there’s a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart.”

“It’ll never close up; I won’t let it. I will miss him & love him for all my days.”

Taylorannounced in November 2022he’d been diagnosed four years earlier withstage four metastatic prostate cancer. His ongoing treatment forced him to miss the band’s induction that year into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.

Beyond his time with Duran Duran, the skilled musician was a dedicated family man who later had a lengthy career as a producer and solo artist.

Duran Duran formed in Birmingham, England, in the late 1970s, and soon after Taylorjoined the band in 1980– he answered their ad for a guitarist in the music weekly Melody Maker – they became one of the most popular bands of the 1980s.

“It was like ‘bang!’” Taylor toldThe Evening Chroniclein 2004 of seeing the ad. At the time, he had been playing in a local band in his hometown of Cullercoats, nearNewcastle, but he wanted to do more.

Mentioning how the music influences cited in the ad aligned with his interests, he told the publication, “I just thought, ‘yeah I can do that.’ There were 20 ads, and it was just that one. It was a bigger ad, so I thought they must have more money, a good sign.”

Fueled in large part byflashy videos in heavy rotation on MTVand a unique blend of synth-pop and rock, Duran Duran’s heavily styled new wave hair, clothes and heartthrob gazes from members Simon Le Bon, John Taylor, Roger Taylor (no relation to Andy) and Nick Rhodes on posters and magazine covers cemented their appeal.

The rhythm guitar came from Taylor, who had already spent a few years as a teenager playing in working men’s clubs in his hometown and at military bases in Germany,where he didsix 45-minute sets a dayfrom a 300-song repertoire. That made him a seasoned, versatile guitarist even before the age of 20, able to handle a variety of genres with ease – and made himstand outfrom dozens of others who’d answered Duran Duran’s ad.

He moved to Birmingham and became one of five members of a band that would help define ‘80s music. His sound was a key part of the band’s first Top 10 single in the UK, “Girls on Film.”

After Duran Duran’s self-titled debut record came the massive success of the albums “Rio” and “Seven and the Ragged Tiger,” which produced the band’s biggest hit – “The Reflex” –reaching No. 1on the US and UK charts in 1984. Other singles including “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “Last Chance on the Stairway” and “The Wild Boys” also showcased Taylor’s guitar.

“In contributing to their sound, it was unique, because it was the new wave electronic period coming out of disco,” said Steve Craig, formerprogram director for Atlanta alternative rock station 99X.

Though Taylor was more of a rock fan when he joined the band, he saw a “magical potential” in that multi-dimensional musical mix, he wrote in his autobiography, “Wild Boy: My Life in Duran Duran.”

In 1984, Taylor and Duran Duran bassist John Taylor formed a side project called The Power Station with good friend Tony Thompson, the drummer for the disco band Chic. The band went on to score two top 10 hits in the US.

“At the time, I felt Andy was really underused,” John Taylortold VH1’s“Behind the Music”in 1999. “I said, ‘We’re going to do something more aggressive next time, you and I.’”

“The music that John and I made in the Power Station was partly born out of frustration at not being able to play the way we wanted to in Duran Duran,” Andy Taylor wrote in his book. “So when the opportunity came along to do something different we seized it with both hands.”

With Duran Duran lead singer Simon Le Bon having embarked on a lengthy sailing trip, and finding himself exhausted from the pressures of fame and constant touring, the late Taylor officially left Duran Duran in 1986. At that point, he’d been in two successful bands and realized his own success didn’t have to be tied to a particular group.

“We did go hard at it in America. Very hard at it. And it took its toll,” Taylor told theRockonteurs podcastin 2023.

It was in the northern England seaside community ofCullercoatsthat Taylor – who came from a family of fishermen and seafarers – first started strumming a guitar. At age 13, he knocked on the door of a neighbor, whom he knew to be a blues and rock guitarist, and flashed a pound coin to ask for lessons.

“This guy showed me all the cool shortcuts. Scales. He showed me all those bloody Stevie Wonder chords … and how they were used melodically,” Taylortold the Rockonteurs podcast. “He was a phenomenal lead guitar player, so every time I sat in front of him, he’d do something and I’d be straight back home in four hours trying to figure it out.”

It turned out the neighbor, Dave Black, was a member of the Spiders from Mars, the backing group for rock legend David Bowie. And the first big turning point in Taylor’s musical life came the day he spotted the band outside his house.

“When that happened, I was about 13 or 14, and it was just there across the road from me. The f**kin’ Spiders from Mars. On my street. And that made me think anything was possible,” Taylor told the podcast.

When Taylor left Duran Duran, he was just 26 – but he knew he wanted to chart his own course making and creating music. He was given a multimillion-dollar record deal in 1986 for a solo album, “Thunder,” a rock record that matched the era but nevertheless languished in the charts.

“That was the first time I met the big F-word: failure,” hetold “Behind the Music.”

But he didn’t stop seeking creative outlets he could pursue on his own terms, and he always came back to the music. Along with his solo albums, Taylor went on to produce dozens of records for everyone from Rod Stewart to English bandThe Ting Tings, and collaborate with artists from The Sex Pistols’ Steve Jones to’80s pop singerBelinda Carlisle.

Taylor rejoined Duran Duran in 2001 for a series of successful concerts and their 2004 album “Astronaut” before quitting again in 2006. He realized he no longer wanted to devote himself to any band full-time.

“I can’t do band rules anymore. I can’t do them,” he said on the Rockonteurs podcast. “And I discovered that second time around, that band rules can’t trump life rules. Family, kids. You know, there’s only so much you can give up.”

He continued, “I just had to come to terms with that – that I did start very young. You know, I was on the road full-time from the age of 16, and by the time I got to 40, putting the band first … you just got to have a word with yourself.”

Taylor leaves behind his wife of 44 years, Tracey Wilson – who was Duran Duran’s hairdresser when they wed – along with four children and a grandchild. Speaking toPeople magazine in 2023, Taylor joked he’d been “married for 40,000 years” and credited the “tolerance” of his wife, saying she ought to win an award for “women who’ve survived rock and roll.”

Wilson called her late husband “the rock of our family” in the official Instagram statement released Wednesday.

“For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home.”

Taylor remained close with Le Bon, who in 2022 traveled to Taylor’s home on the Spanish island of Ibiza to personally deliver the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame award that his friend wasn’t able to accept in person.

At the induction ceremony, Le Bon read aloud part of a letter Taylor had written for the event that looked back on the “beyond incredible” years they spent together.

“Literally from the day I met Nick, John, Simon and Roger they truly valued the contribution of a rather noisy, versatile Northern brat,” Taylorwrote.

“I loved going into the studio and recording our material; nobody else sounded like us.”

Taylor added he was “massively disappointed” that his cancer treatment at the time forced him to miss the induction ceremony.

“I’m so very proud of these four brothers,” he wrote. “I’m amazed at their durability, and I’m overjoyed at accepting this award. I often doubted the day would come. I’m sure as hell glad I’m around to see the day.”

Intheir official statementthis week, Duran Duran said Taylor “was there at the very beginning of our story,” adding that “he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.”

“His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”
